name: Willow bark extract

lead: Willow bark extract comes from Salix species and contains salicin, which the body converts to salicylate. It has a long history as a traditional pain and fever remedy and is the historical source of salicylic acid chemistry.

Skincare brands sometimes use it as a 'natural salicylic acid' for acne or exfoliation. The clinical trials found are all oral studies in pain conditions, so skin claims are untested in those sources.

paras: Salicin is a glucoside; after ingestion it is metabolised to salicylic acid derivatives. Reviews note that polyphenols and flavonoids in the extract may also contribute to anti-inflammatory effects.
Salicylates are toxic in excess, and salicylate-containing products carry labelled cautions. Topical cosmetic willow extracts have little dedicated safety literature in the sources reviewed.

label.generic: GLUCOSAMINE SULFATE POTASSIUM CHLORIDE,WHITE WILLOW BARK EXTRACT,EGGSHELL MEMBRANE COLLAGEN,CHONDROITIN SULFATE,TURMERIC ROOT EXTRACT,BROMELAIN,SOY LECITHIN

lead: Willow bark extract is a preparation from the bark of willow trees, most often white willow (Salix alba), containing the glucoside salicin along with polyphenols.[1][2] Salicin was isolated in crystalline form in 1828, and salicylic acid is derived from it chemically.[1][3]

The extract is used orally in Europe for pain, and in skincare it is promoted as a botanical source of salicylic acid.[2] Published human trials in the sources reviewed concern oral use in low back pain and osteoarthritis, not skin appearance.[4][5]
infobox: Bark of Salix species (e.g. S. alba)

paras: In 1763 Edward Stone of Oxfordshire reported using powdered willow bark to treat fevers in about fifty people over several years, though Wikipedia notes the medical profession largely ignored this at the time.[1] Salicin was isolated by Henri Leroux and Raffaele Piria in 1828, while Wikipedia's salicylic acid entry credits Johann Andreas Buchner that year; Piria later obtained salicylic acid from it.[1][3] Aspirin itself is a synthetic derivative and does not occur in nature.[1]

Skincare brands describe willow bark extract as a gentler plant-derived alternative to salicylic acid for blemish-prone skin. Salicylic acid itself is an established keratolytic used for acne and other skin conditions,[3] but the sources reviewed do not include trials showing that willow bark extract in a topical product delivers comparable effects.
Oral standardised extracts are used in Europe for low back pain and osteoarthritis.[4][5]

A randomised double-blind study enrolled 210 patients with exacerbations of chronic low back pain and tested an oral willow bark extract.[4] A 2015 review concluded that a small number of clinical studies support its use in chronic low back and joint pain and osteoarthritis, while noting few studies overall.[2] A placebo-controlled trial in osteoarthritis and systematic reviews of herbal anti-inflammatory drugs also exist.[5][6] A registered trial of a multi-ingredient product listing Salix alba studied anxiety, not skin.[7] No studies on topical willow bark extract for appearance were found.

Wikipedia notes that salicylates in excess are toxic and that cosmetic salicylic acid use has been judged by one cited study not to pose significant systemic risk; it also lists hazards such as eye damage on the pure acid.[3] A US supplement label containing white willow bark extract is on file with DailyMed.[8]

timeline.event: Edward Stone reports willow bark use for fevers.[1]
